title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon
summary:
Bomb: The Race to Build—and Steal—the World's Most Dangerous Weapon is a 2012 adolescent non-fiction book by author Steve Sheinkin. The book won the 2013 Newbery Honor and Sibert Medal from the American Library Association.
This book follows the process of building the nuclear bomb by the discovery of nuclear fission by German scientist Otto Hahn on December 17, 1938.

pieces.name: Adolf Hitler
pieces.sentence:
Rapid Rupture: 33
Hitler's character in "Bomb" represents more than just a historical figure - he embodies the existential threat that justifies the development of ultimate weapons. His persecution of scientists inadvertently helped the Allies while his aggressive expansionism made atomic weapons seem necessary to prevent global domination by a totalitarian regime.

In Sheinkin's narrative, Hitler serves as the absent but ever-present catalyst whose actions set every major plotline in motion. His anti-Semitic policies scattered brilliant scientists across the world, his territorial ambitions made war inevitable, and his potential access to atomic weapons made the Manhattan Project seem like humanity's only hope for survival. The tragic irony is that Hitler's own prejudices and poor leadership probably ensured that Nazi Germany never came close to building the very weapons that his enemies developed specifically to stop him.
pieces.about: Adolf Hitler was an Austrian-born German politician who was the dictator of Germany during the Nazi period from 1933 until his suicide in 1945. He rose to power as the leader of the Nazi Party, becoming the chancellor in 1933 and then taking the title of Führer und Reichskanzler in 1934. His invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 marked the start of the Second World War. He was closely involved in military operations throughout the war and was central to the perpetration of the Holocaust: the genocide of about six million Jews and millions of other victims.

pieces.name: Albert Einstein
pieces.sentence:
Finding Einstein: 19
Epilogue: Scorpions in a Bottle: 231

Einstein serves as the crucial catalyst figure in Sheinkin's narrative - the world-famous scientist whose single signature transforms a theoretical possibility into a massive government program. The "Einstein-Szilard letter to President Roosevelt changed the course of history by prompting American government involvement in nuclear research" and "led to the establishment of the Manhattan Project".
His character embodies one of the central themes of "Bomb" - how well-intentioned actions in wartime can have devastating and unforeseen consequences that haunt their creators long after victory is achieved. Einstein's deep regret serves as a moral counterpoint to the scientific triumph and wartime necessity that drive the main narrative forward.
pieces.about: Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist who is widely held as one of the most influential scientists. Best known for developing the theory of relativity, Einstein also made important contributions to quantum mechanics. His mass–energy equivalence formula E = mc2, which arises from relativity theory, has been called "the world's most famous equation". He received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics "for his services to theoretical physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect", a pivotal step in the development of quantum theory. His intellectual achievements and originality have made the word Einstein broadly synonymous with genius.

pieces.name: Alexander Sachs
pieces.sentence:
Finding Einstein: 20
Alexander Sachs serves as the crucial political bridge between the scientific community and government power in Sheinkin's "Bomb." "The Einstein-Szilard letter to President Roosevelt changed the course of history by prompting American government involvement in nuclear research. The letter led to the establishment of the Manhattan Project", and Sachs was the messenger who made this possible.
In "Bomb," Alexander Sachs embodies the crucial role of political communication in turning scientific discoveries into national policy. His character shows how the atomic age required not just brilliant scientists, but also skilled communicators who could bridge the gap between theoretical physics and practical politics. Without Sachs's persistence, timing, and persuasive skills, Einstein's letter might have been filed away rather than launching the Manhattan Project.
Sachs represents the often-overlooked figures who make history possible through their ability to communicate effectively with power. His immigrant background connects him to the broader theme of how refugee scientists and their allies transformed American scientific capabilities, while his economic expertise and political savvy demonstrate the interdisciplinary nature of the effort that created atomic weapons.
pieces.about: Alexander Sachs was an American economist and banker. In October 1939 he delivered the Einstein–Szilard letter to President Franklin D. Roosevelt, suggesting that nuclear-fission research ought to be pursued with a view to possibly constructing nuclear weapons, should they prove feasible, in view of the likelihood that Nazi Germany would do so. This led to the initiation of the United States' Manhattan Project.

pieces.about: Amtorg Trading Corporation, also known as Amtorg, was the first trade representation of the Soviet Union in the United States, established in New York in 1924 by merging Armand Hammer's Allied American Corporation (Alamerico) with Products Exchange Corporation (Prodexco) and Arcos-America Inc..

Anatoli Yatskov represents the sophisticated Soviet intelligence operation that successfully penetrated the Manhattan Project, showing how the race to build atomic weapons involved not just scientific competition but also a parallel intelligence war, and demonstrating how effective espionage helped transform the Soviet Union into a nuclear superpower.
pieces.about: Anatoly Antonovich Yatskov, also known as Anatoli Yatzkov – was a Soviet consul in New York as well as an NKVD foreign intelligence officer handling American agents and couriers linked to the U.S. Manhattan Project during WWII. His spy cover was eventually blown by the U.S. Army Venona Program which identified him as a key NKVD spymaster involved in the 1940s Atomic Spy Ring.

Arne Kjelstrup plays an important role in the Norwegian resistance storyline that forms a crucial part of Sheinkin's "Bomb":

Operation Gunnerside Participant: Kjelstrup was one of the Norwegian saboteurs who successfully destroyed the heavy water electrolysis cells at the Vemork plant in February 1943. This operation was crucial in denying Nazi Germany the materials needed for atomic research.
Local Knowledge: His understanding of the local terrain, weather, and conditions was essential for the team's ability to approach the heavily guarded facility and execute their mission successfully.
Survival and Escape: After the successful sabotage mission, Kjelstrup had to survive the dangerous escape across occupied Norwegian territory, evading German patrols and surviving in harsh winter conditions.
David vs. Goliath Theme: Kjelstrup's story embodies Sheinkin's broader theme about how small groups of determined individuals could have enormous impact on the atomic weapons race. His actions helped prevent Nazi atomic weapons development.
International Resistance: Through Kjelstrup's experiences, Sheinkin demonstrates how the race for atomic weapons involved not just scientists and military leaders, but also ordinary citizens who became heroes in the fight against fascism.

Kjelstrup represents the brave Norwegian resistance fighters whose local knowledge, courage, and dedication were essential to the successful sabotage operations that helped prevent Nazi Germany from obtaining materials crucial for atomic weapons development.
pieces.about: Arne Kjelstrup, MM was a Norwegian resistance member during World War II, especially noted for his role in the heavy water sabotage 1942–1943, and for being military leader of Milorg section D-161 (Kongsberg/Numedal) during the anti-demolition operation Sunshine 1944–1945.

pieces.about: Boris Theodore Pash was a United States Army military intelligence officer. He commanded the Alsos Mission during World War II and retired with the rank of colonel.

pieces.name: Brehon Somervell
pieces.about: Brehon Burke Somervell was a general in the United States Army and Commanding General of the Army Service Forces in World War II. As such he was responsible for the U.S. Army's logistics. Following his death, The Washington Post lauded him as "one of the ablest officers the United States Army has produced".

pieces.name: British Royal Air Force
pieces.about: The Royal Air Force (RAF) is the air and space force of the United Kingdom, British Overseas Territories and Crown Dependencies. It was formed towards the end of the First World War on 1 April 1918, on the merger of the Royal Flying Corps (RFC) and the Royal Naval Air Service (RNAS). Following the Allied victory over the Central Powers in 1918, the RAF emerged as the largest air force in the world at the time. Since its formation, the RAF has played a significant role in British military history. In particular, during the Second World War, the RAF established air superiority over Nazi Germany's Luftwaffe during the Battle of Britain, and led the Allied strategic bombing effort.

pieces.name: Bruno Rossi
pieces.sentence:
Born Rebel: 132

Bruno Rossi embodies the international community of refugee scientists whose persecution by fascist regimes ironically strengthened the Allied effort to develop atomic weapons, representing how the Manhattan Project benefited from the scientific talent that fled Europe and found refuge in America, where their expertise was crucial to creating the weapons that would help defeat fascism.
pieces.about: Bruno Benedetto Rossi was an Italian-American experimental physicist. He made major contributions to particle physics and the study of cosmic rays. A 1927 graduate of the University of Bologna, he became interested in cosmic rays. To study them, he invented an improved electronic coincidence circuit, and travelled to Eritrea to conduct experiments that showed that cosmic ray intensity from the West was significantly larger than that from the East.

Carl Eifler plays an important role in the intelligence and sabotage aspects of Sheinkin's story about the race for atomic weapons:

OSS Operations: As a leader in the Office of Strategic Services (OSS), America's wartime intelligence agency, Eifler was involved in planning and executing covert operations designed to disrupt enemy atomic research and gather intelligence about German and Japanese nuclear programs.
Kidnapping Mission Plans: One of the most dramatic elements of Eifler's story involves proposed missions to kidnap key German atomic scientists, including Werner Heisenberg. These plans illustrate the desperate measures the Allies were willing to consider to prevent Nazi atomic weapons development.
Intelligence Gathering: Eifler's operations provided crucial intelligence about the status of enemy atomic research, helping Allied leaders understand whether they were winning or losing the race to build the bomb.
Parallel Action: While scientists like Oppenheimer were building America's atomic weapons, Eifler represents the military/intelligence side of the story - the efforts to sabotage enemy programs and gather vital information about their progress.

Eifler embodies the world of espionage, sabotage, and special operations that ran parallel to the scientific efforts, showing how the atomic bomb race involved not just laboratory work but also dangerous covert missions around the world.
pieces.about: Carl Frederick Eifler was a U.S. Army officer best known for having commanded Detachment 101, which served behind the enemy lines in Japanese-occupied Burma during World War II. He helped stand up 13 army reserve detachments outside major universities to preserve the expertise and knowledge of the returning GIs.

pieces.name: Carl von Weizsäcker
pieces.about: Carl Friedrich Freiherr von Weizsäcker was a German physicist and philosopher. He was the longest-living member of the team which performed nuclear research in Nazi Germany during the Second World War, under Werner Heisenberg's leadership. There is ongoing debate as to whether or not he and the other members of the team actively and willingly pursued the development of a nuclear bomb for Germany during this time.

pieces.name: Charles Sweeney
pieces.sentence:
Reactions Begin: 205

Charles Sweeney plays a crucial role in Steve Sheinkin's "Bomb" as one of the key military figures in the actual deployment of atomic weapons:
Nagasaki Mission Pilot - Sweeney piloted "Bockscar," the B-29 that dropped the plutonium bomb "Fat Man" on Nagasaki on August 9, 1945, making him central to the book's climactic moments.
Hiroshima Mission Participant - He also flew the observation plane during the Hiroshima bombing mission on August 6, 1945, giving him direct involvement in both atomic bombings.
Military Execution - His role represents the military side of the atomic bomb story, showing how years of scientific development ultimately required skilled pilots and crews to deliver these weapons to their targets.
Technical Challenges - Sheinkin uses Sweeney's missions to illustrate the practical difficulties of atomic bombing, including mechanical problems, weather issues, and fuel concerns that made these missions far from routine.
Human Face of Destruction - Through Sweeney's perspective, the book shows how individual servicemen carried out orders that would kill hundreds of thousands of people and end World War II.
Completion of the Project - Sweeney's successful missions represent the final step in the Manhattan Project, transforming years of scientific research into military action that changed world history.

Sheinkin uses Sweeney's story to bridge the gap between the scientific development of atomic weapons and their actual use in warfare, showing how the theoretical became devastatingly real.
pieces.about: Charles William Sweeney was an officer in the United States Army Air Forces during World War II and the pilot who flew Bockscar carrying the Fat Man atomic bomb to the Japanese city of Nagasaki on 9 August 1945. Separating from active duty at the end of World War II, he later became an officer in the Massachusetts Air National Guard as the Army Air Forces transitioned to an independent United States Air Force, eventually rising to the rank of major general.

pieces.name: Charlotte Serber
pieces.sentence:
Rapid Rupture: 34
The Gatekeeper: 94
Charlotte serves several important functions in Sheinkin's account:  As the librarian and manager of classified documents at Los Alamos, Charlotte was responsible for controlling access to the scientific papers, reports, and technical documents that contained the secrets of atomic weapons development. This made her a crucial figure in maintaining project security.
Behind-the-Scenes Perspective: Through Charlotte's role, Sheinkin illustrates how the Manhattan Project required not just brilliant scientists, but also dedicated support staff who could handle the complex logistics and security requirements of such a massive secret undertaking.
Symbol of Sacrifice: Like many spouses of Manhattan Project scientists, Charlotte represents the personal sacrifices made by families who lived in isolation at Los Alamos, maintaining secrecy while supporting the war effort.
Window into Daily Life: Her experiences provide insight into what life was like for the community at Los Alamos, showing how ordinary people contributed to this extraordinary project.

Charlotte Serber represents the essential but often overlooked support personnel who made the Manhattan Project possible through their dedication and trustworthiness.
pieces.about: Charlotte Serber was an American journalist, statistician and librarian. She was the librarian of the Manhattan Project's Los Alamos Laboratory during World War II, and the laboratory's only female group leader. After the war she attempted to secure a position as a librarian at the Radiation Laboratory in Berkeley, but was rejected for lack of a security clearance; the likely reason was due to her political views. She later became a production assistant for the Broadway Theatre, and an interviewer for Louis Harris.

pieces.about: Clarence Francis Hiskey (1912–1998), born Clarence Szczechowski, was a scientist who worked on the Manhattan Project and was identified as Soviet espionage agent. He became active in the Communist Party USA (CPUSA) when he attended graduate school at the University of Wisconsin.

Claus Helberg plays an important role in one of the most dramatic storylines in Sheinkin's "Bomb" - the Norwegian resistance operations against German heavy water production:

Gunnerside Team Member: Helberg was part of the Norwegian sabotage team (codenamed "Gunnerside") that successfully destroyed the heavy water electrolysis cells at the Vemork plant in February 1943. This operation was crucial in preventing Nazi Germany from obtaining materials needed for atomic research.
Escape and Survival: After the successful sabotage mission, Helberg undertook a harrowing escape across hundreds of miles of occupied Norwegian territory, skiing through enemy patrols and surviving in brutal winter conditions. His escape story demonstrates the incredible risks taken by resistance fighters.
Local Knowledge: As a Norwegian native familiar with the local terrain and conditions, Helberg provided essential knowledge that made the sabotage mission possible. His understanding of the landscape, weather patterns, and local conditions was crucial to the operation's success.
David vs. Goliath Theme: Helberg's story embodies Sheinkin's broader theme about how small groups of determined individuals could have enormous impact on the atomic weapons race. His actions helped deny crucial materials to the Nazi atomic program.
International Resistance: Through Helberg's experiences, Sheinkin shows how the race for atomic weapons involved not just scientists and military leaders, but also ordinary citizens who became extraordinary heroes in the fight against fascism.

Helberg represents the brave resistance fighters whose dangerous missions and personal sacrifices were essential to preventing Nazi atomic weapons development.
pieces.about: Claus Helberg was a Norwegian resistance fighter and mountain guide. He was a member of Company Linge, a resistance commando unit that was best known for carrying out Norwegian heavy water sabotage during World War II. After the war, he worked for the Norwegian Mountain Touring Association until his retirement in 1982. While volunteering with the Association after his retirement, he helped guide several members of the Scandinavian royalty. According to The New York Times, "[he was] the favorite mountain guide of Scandinavian royalty..." These clients included Queen Sonja and Margrethe II of Denmark.

pieces.name: Columbia University
pieces.about: Columbia University in the City of New York, commonly referred to as Columbia University, is a private Ivy League research university in New York City. Established in 1754 as King's College on the grounds of Trinity Church in Manhattan, it is the oldest institution of higher education in New York and the fifth-oldest in the United States.

pieces.name: Counter Intelligence Corps (CIC)
pieces.about: The Counter Intelligence Corps was a World War II and early Cold War intelligence agency within the United States Army consisting of highly trained special agents. Its role was taken over by the U.S. Army Intelligence Corps in 1961 and, in 1967, by the United States Army Intelligence Agency. Its functions are now performed by its modern-day descendant organization, United States Army Counterintelligence. The National Counter Intelligence Corps Association (NCICA), a veterans' association, was established in the years immediately following World War II by former military intelligence agents.

pieces.name: David Greenglass
pieces.sentence:

David Greenglass plays a significant role in Steve Sheinkin's "Bomb" as one of the key atomic spies who provided crucial information to the Soviet Union:

Manhattan Project Insider - Greenglass worked as a machinist at Los Alamos, where he had access to sensitive information about the atomic bomb's construction, particularly the implosion device used in the plutonium bomb.
Soviet Spy Network - He was recruited into espionage by his brother-in-law Julius Rosenberg and passed detailed sketches and technical information about the bomb's design to Soviet agents.
Key Intelligence Source - The information Greenglass provided, including drawings of the implosion lens system, significantly helped Soviet scientists understand crucial aspects of atomic bomb construction.
Family Spy Ring - His story illustrates how the atomic espionage network operated through family connections, with his wife Ruth and sister Ethel also involved in the spy operations.
Turning Witness - After being caught, Greenglass became a government witness, and his testimony was crucial in the prosecution of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, demonstrating how the atomic spy cases ultimately tore families apart.

Sheinkin uses Greenglass's story to show how ordinary people became part of the massive intelligence operation that gave the Soviet Union critical atomic secrets, accelerating their bomb development and intensifying the Cold War nuclear arms race.
pieces.about: David Greenglass was an American machinist who worked on the Manhattan Project and was an atomic spy for the Soviet Union. He was briefly stationed at the Clinton Engineer Works uranium enrichment facility at Oak Ridge, Tennessee, and then worked at the Los Alamos Laboratory in New Mexico from August 1944 until February 1946.

pieces.name: David Lilienthal
pieces.sentence:

Sheinkin uses Lilienthal's story to illustrate the road not taken - the possibility that atomic energy might have been placed under international control rather than becoming the foundation for a nuclear arms race, and to show how postwar idealism about atomic cooperation gave way to Cold War competition.
pieces.about: David Eli Lilienthal was an American attorney and public administrator, best known for his presidential appointment to head Tennessee Valley Authority and later the Atomic Energy Commission (AEC). He had practiced public utility law and led the Wisconsin Public Utilities Commission.

pieces.about: Frederick Henry Derek Curtis-Bennett, QC was a British barrister who defended some of the most notorious characters in British legal history, but whose career was cut short by alcoholism. His father was Sir Henry Curtis-Bennett KC, whose biography he wrote with Roland Wild.

pieces.about: A doctor, also known as a physician, is a medical professional who is trained to diagnose and treat illnesses, injuries, and other health conditions. Doctors play a crucial role in maintaining public health, providing care and advice to patients, and advancing medical knowledge through research. Doctors are vital to the healthcare system, dedicated to diagnosing, treating, and preventing illnesses to improve patient health and well-being. The path to becoming a doctor is rigorous, requiring extensive education and training, but the profession is highly rewarding, offering the opportunity to make a significant impact on people's lives. As medical science and technology continue to evolve, the role of doctors will also adapt, ensuring that they remain at the forefront of providing high-quality healthcare.

Donald Hornig plays an important technical role in Sheinkin's account of the Manhattan Project:

Firing Unit Development: Hornig worked specifically on the firing unit at Los Alamos, which was crucial for the proper detonation of atomic bombs. His work ensured that the complex timing and explosive sequences would function correctly when needed.
Trinity Test Involvement: Hornig was involved in the preparations for the Trinity test, the first atomic bomb explosion in New Mexico. His expertise with firing mechanisms was essential to making sure the test device would detonate properly.
Technical Expertise: Through Hornig's work, Sheinkin illustrates the incredibly complex engineering challenges involved in creating functional atomic weapons. It wasn't enough to understand the physics - scientists also needed to solve practical problems of timing, explosives, and mechanical precision.
Young Scientists' Contribution: Hornig represents the many young, talented scientists who contributed specialized skills to the Manhattan Project. His story shows how the atomic bomb required not just famous physicists like Oppenheimer, but also skilled chemists, engineers, and other specialists.
High-Stakes Engineering: Hornig's work on firing units demonstrates how every component of the atomic bomb had to work perfectly, as there would be no second chances once the weapons were deployed in combat.

Donald Hornig embodies the skilled technical specialists whose precise, behind-the-scenes work was essential to transforming theoretical physics into functioning weapons, showing how the Manhattan Project required diverse expertise beyond just nuclear physics to succeed.
pieces.about: Donald Frederick Hornig was an American chemist, explosives expert, teacher and presidential science advisor. He served as president of Brown University from 1970 to 1976.

pieces.name: Dorothy McKibben
pieces.sentence:
The Gatekeeper: 91
Born Rebel: 132

Dorothy McKibben plays an important supporting role in Sheinkin's account of the Manhattan Project:

Administrative Hub: As Oppenheimer's assistant, McKibben served as a crucial link in the administrative chain that kept Los Alamos functioning. Her work ensured that the practical, day-to-day operations of the laboratory ran smoothly.
Gateway to Los Alamos: McKibben often served as one of the first contacts for new arrivals at Los Alamos, helping to orient scientists and staff to the secret facility and its unique requirements.
Behind-the-Scenes Support: Through McKibben's role, Sheinkin illustrates how the Manhattan Project required not just brilliant scientists, but also dedicated support staff who could handle the complex logistics of running a secret research facility.
Human Element: McKibben represents the many civilian employees who contributed essential skills to the Manhattan Project while maintaining the secrecy and security necessary for the operation's success.
Organizational Infrastructure: Her work demonstrates how the atomic bomb required not just scientific breakthroughs, but also efficient administrative systems to coordinate resources, personnel, and information across the vast Manhattan Project.

Dorothy McKibben embodies the dedicated support personnel whose organizational skills and administrative expertise were essential to the Manhattan Project's success, showing how the development of atomic weapons required diverse talents beyond just scientific research, including the crucial behind-the-scenes work that kept the entire operation functioning effectively.
pieces.about: Dorothy McKibbin worked on the Manhattan Project during World War II. She ran the project's office at 109 East Palace Avenue in Santa Fe, through which staff moving to the Los Alamos Laboratory had to pass through to obtain security credentials and directions to their new workplace. She was known as the "first lady of Los Alamos", and was often the first point of contact for new arrivals. She retired when the Santa Fe office closed in 1963.

pieces.name: Douglas MacArthur
pieces.sentence:
Laboratory Number 2: 103
Douglas MacArthur embodies the military leadership perspective that viewed atomic weapons as strategic tools for ending the war quickly and saving American lives, representing the military context within which the decision to use the atomic bombs was ultimately made and executed.
pieces.about: Douglas MacArthur was an American general who served as a top commander during World War II and the Korean War, achieving the rank of General of the Army. He served with distinction in World War I; as chief of staff of the United States Army from 1930 to 1935; as Supreme Commander, Southwest Pacific Area, from 1942 to 1945 during WWII; as Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers overseeing the occupation of Japan from 1945 to 1951; and as head of the United Nations Command in the Korean War from 1950 to 1951. MacArthur was nominated for the Medal of Honor three times, and awarded it for his WWII service in the Philippines. He is one of only five people to hold the rank of General of the Army, and the only person to hold the rank of Field Marshal in the Philippine Army.

Dr. Norman Ramsey embodies the skilled physicists whose technical expertise and methodical approach were essential to solving the engineering challenges of atomic weapons development, representing how the Manhattan Project required scientists who could focus on both theoretical understanding and practical implementation to create functional nuclear weapons.
pieces.about: Norman Foster Ramsey Jr. was an American physicist who was awarded the 1989 Nobel Prize in Physics for the invention of the separated oscillatory field method, which had important applications in the construction of atomic clocks. A physics professor at Harvard University for most of his career, Ramsey also held several posts with such government and international agencies as NATO and the United States Atomic Energy Commission. Among his other accomplishments are helping to found the United States Department of Energy's Brookhaven National Laboratory and Fermilab.

Oppenheimer offered Gerjuoy a position working with him at Los Alamos to help the production of the atomic bomb, but Gerjuoy refused…

Edward Teller embodies the scientists whose brilliant minds could envision weapons of unprecedented destruction, while also representing the challenges of managing diverse personalities and competing priorities within the Manhattan Project, and foreshadowing the nuclear arms race that would define the Cold War era.
pieces.about: Edward Teller was a Hungarian-American theoretical physicist and chemical engineer who is known colloquially as "the father of the hydrogen bomb" and one of the creators of the Teller–Ulam design inspired by Stanisław Ulam. He had a volatile personality, and was "driven by his megaton ambitions, had a messianic complex, and displayed autocratic behavior." He devised a thermonuclear Alarm Clock bomb with a yield of 1000 MT and proposed delivering it by boat or submarine to incinerate a continent.

pieces.name: Eleanor Roosevelt
pieces.about: Anna Eleanor Roosevelt was an American political figure, diplomat, and activist. She was the longest-serving first lady of the United States, during her husband Franklin D. Roosevelt's four terms as president from 1933 to 1945. Through her travels, public engagement, and advocacy, she largely redefined the role. Widowed in 1945, she served as a United States delegate to the United Nations General Assembly from 1945 to 1952, and took a leading role in designing the text and gaining international support for the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. In 1948, she was given a standing ovation by the assembly upon their adoption of the declaration. President Harry S. Truman later called her the "First Lady of the World" in tribute to her human rights achievements.

pieces.name: Emilio Segre
pieces.about: Emilio Gino Segrè was an Italian-American nuclear physicist and radiochemist who discovered the elements technetium and astatine, and the antiproton, a subatomic antiparticle, for which he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1959, along with Owen Chamberlain.

Enrico Fermi plays several pivotal roles in Sheinkin's account of the atomic bomb development:

First Nuclear Chain Reaction: Fermi's most crucial contribution was achieving the first controlled nuclear chain reaction at the University of Chicago in December 1942. This experiment proved that atomic energy could be harnessed and controlled, making the atomic bomb theoretically possible.
Scientific Foundation: His work provided the fundamental proof of concept that underpinned the entire Manhattan Project. Without Fermi's successful chain reaction, the massive investment in atomic weapons development might never have occurred.
Los Alamos Contributor: At Los Alamos, Fermi continued to play a key role in weapons design and testing, bringing his unique combination of theoretical knowledge and practical skills to the bomb development effort.
Moral Complexity: Fermi represents the scientists who, despite understanding the devastating implications of their work, continued to pursue atomic weapons development out of scientific curiosity and wartime necessity. His story illustrates the moral dilemmas faced by scientists during the Manhattan Project.
International Dimension: As an Italian refugee who fled fascist Europe, Fermi's story also represents how the brain drain from Nazi-occupied Europe strengthened American atomic research while weakening Axis scientific capabilities.

Fermi embodies the brilliant scientific mind whose breakthrough discoveries made atomic weapons possible, while also representing the complex moral position of scientists who created weapons of unprecedented destructive power.
pieces.about: Enrico Fermi was an Italian and naturalized American physicist, renowned for being the creator of the world's first artificial nuclear reactor, the Chicago Pile-1, and a member of the Manhattan Project. He has been called the "architect of the nuclear age" and the "architect of the atomic bomb". He was one of very few physicists to excel in both theoretical and experimental physics. Fermi was awarded the 1938 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on induced radioactivity by neutron bombardment and for the discovery of transuranium elements. With his colleagues, Fermi filed several patents related to the use of nuclear power, all of which were taken over by the US government. He made significant contributions to the development of statistical mechanics, quantum theory, and nuclear and particle physics.

Roosevelt appears as the essential catalyst who makes the American atomic program possible. Roosevelt's death in April 1945 becomes a pivotal moment in Sheinkin's narrative, as he "had left Truman no documentation or policy directives" about how to use the bomb. Einstein had sent a second letter in March 1945 expressing concerns about nuclear weapons, and a meeting between physicist Leo Szilard and FDR was scheduled for May, but "the meeting never happened, because on April 12, the president died of a stroke".
This timing creates dramatic tension in Sheinkin's narrative, as Roosevelt - the leader who initiated the Manhattan Project - never lives to see the completion of the weapon or grapple with the moral implications of its use. His character represents the intersection of scientific possibility and political power that drives the entire "race to build and steal the world's most dangerous weapon."
pieces.about: Franklin Delano Roosevelt, also known as FDR, was the 32nd president of the United States, serving from 1933 until his death in 1945. He is the longest-serving U.S. president, and the only one to have served more than two terms. His first two terms were centered on combating the Great Depression, while his third and fourth saw him shift his focus to America's involvement in World War II.

pieces.about: George Catlett Marshall Jr. was an American army officer and statesman. He rose through the United States Army to become Chief of Staff of the U.S. Army under presidents Franklin D. Roosevelt and Harry S. Truman, then served as Secretary of State and Secretary of Defense under Truman. Winston Churchill lauded Marshall as the "organizer of victory" for his leadership of the Allied victory in World War II. During the subsequent year, he unsuccessfully tried to prevent the continuation of the Chinese Civil War. As Secretary of State, Marshall advocated for a U.S. economic and political commitment to post-war European recovery, including the Marshall Plan that bore his name. In recognition of this work, he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1953, the only Army general ever to receive the honor.

George Weil plays a crucial but often overlooked role in Sheinkin's account of the Manhattan Project:

Historic First Chain Reaction: On December 2, 1942, Weil was the last scientist on the floor who methodically pulled out the cadmium rods as instructed by Fermi, leading to the world's first controlled, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction. This was the pivotal moment that proved atomic weapons were possible.
The Critical Moment: After a break for lunch, Fermi ordered Weil to pull the final cadmium rod out of the pile another 12 inches, and Fermi told Arthur Holly Compton, "This is going to do it. Now it will become self-sustaining". Weil's steady hands literally made nuclear history.
Unsung Hero: Weil represents the many scientists whose contributions were essential but who didn't become household names like Oppenheimer or Fermi. His story illustrates how the Manhattan Project depended on dedicated individuals at every level.
Technical Foundation: Through his work on the experimental Sigma piles, Weil helped develop the technical knowledge and procedures that made the successful CP-1 experiment possible.
Symbol of Responsibility: While Fermi gets credit as the scientific leader, Weil was literally the hands that controlled the reaction, representing the trust placed in individual scientists to carry out procedures that could determine success or catastrophic failure.

George Weil embodies the dedicated, skilled technicians and scientists whose steady work and reliable execution of complex procedures were absolutely essential to the Manhattan Project's success. His role in the first controlled nuclear chain reaction represents a pivotal moment in human history, showing how individual actions by relatively unknown people can literally change the world.
pieces.about: George Leon Weil was an American physicist. On December 2, 1942, he removed the control rod from the Chicago Pile-1 nuclear reactor, initiating the first man-made, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction.

Chevalier plays a crucial role in the book's exploration of loyalty, betrayal, and the security concerns surrounding the Manhattan Project. His connection to the story centers on a controversial incident where he allegedly approached Oppenheimer about passing scientific information to the Soviet Union through intermediaries. This incident later became a major factor in the government's investigation of Oppenheimer's loyalty and contributed to the security hearings that would eventually damage Oppenheimer's career and reputation.
The Chevalier affair, as it came to be known, illustrates the broader themes in Sheinkin's book about how wartime paranoia, shifting political allegiances, and the immense secrecy surrounding atomic weapons development created an atmosphere of suspicion that affected even close personal relationships.
pieces.about: Haakon Maurice Chevalier was an American writer, translator, and professor of French literature at the University of California, Berkeley best known for his friendship with physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, whom he met at Berkeley, California in 1937.

pieces.about: Harlan Fiske Stone was an American attorney who served as an associate justice of the U.S. Supreme Court from 1925 to 1941 and then as the 12th chief justice of the United States from 1941 until his death in 1946. He also served as the U.S. Attorney General from 1924 to 1925 under President Calvin Coolidge, with whom he had attended Amherst College as a young man. His most famous dictum was that "Courts are not the only agency of government that must be assumed to have capacity to govern."

Harry Truman plays a crucial role in the final and most consequential chapters of Sheinkin's "Bomb":

Sudden Responsibility: Truman inherited the Manhattan Project when he became president after Roosevelt's death, representing how this momentous decision fell to someone who had been largely kept in the dark about atomic weapons development.
The Ultimate Decision: Truman made the final decision to use atomic bombs against Japan, making him the only person in history to authorize the use of nuclear weapons in warfare. This decision ended World War II but also ushered in the nuclear age.
Military Strategy: Working with military leaders, Truman weighed the projected casualties from Operation Downfall (the planned invasion of Japan) against using atomic weapons, ultimately choosing the bombs as the option that would end the war most quickly.
Post-War Nuclear Policy: Truman's administration had to grapple with the implications of atomic weapons for international relations, leading to the nuclear arms race with the Soviet Union and the beginning of the Cold War.
Conflict with Scientists: Truman's dismissive attitude toward Oppenheimer's moral concerns illustrated the growing tension between political leaders who saw atomic weapons as tools of statecraft and scientists who understood their unprecedented destructive potential.
Historical Legacy: Through Truman's story, Sheinkin shows how the decision to use atomic weapons created lasting moral and political questions that continue to this day, while also demonstrating the enormous burden of nuclear decision-making that would define the Cold War era.

Harry Truman represents the political leadership that had to make the ultimate decisions about atomic weapons, embodying the perspective that viewed nuclear bombs as necessary tools for ending the war and protecting American interests, while also showing how the atomic bomb immediately transformed international relations and presidential responsibilities.
pieces.about: Harry S. Truman was the 33rd president of the United States, serving from 1945 to 1953. A member of the Democratic Party, he previously served as a United States senator from Missouri from 1935 to 1945 and briefly as the 34th vice president in 1945 under Franklin D. Roosevelt. Assuming the presidency after Roosevelt's death, Truman implemented the Marshall Plan in the wake of World War II to rebuild the economy of Western Europe and established both the Truman Doctrine and NATO to contain the expansion of Soviet communism. He proposed numerous liberal domestic reforms, but few were enacted by the conservative coalition that dominated the Congress.

Herbert Anderson plays several important roles in Sheinkin's account of the Manhattan Project:
First Chain Reaction: Anderson was a key member of Fermi's team that achieved the first controlled nuclear chain reaction at Chicago Pile-1 on December 2, 1942. This was a crucial milestone that proved atomic weapons were possible and marked a turning point in the Manhattan Project.
Trinity Test: Anderson participated in the first atomic bomb test and helped develop methods for measuring the nuclear yield, contributing to the final validation of the atomic weapon before its use in combat.
Scientific Continuity: Anderson represents the scientists who worked on the Manhattan Project from its earliest experimental stages through to the final weapons testing, providing continuity and technical expertise throughout the entire development process.

Herbert Anderson embodies the dedicated nuclear physicists whose technical expertise and collaborative work were essential to every phase of the Manhattan Project, from the initial understanding of nuclear fission through the successful development and testing of atomic weapons. His story illustrates how the atomic bomb required sustained scientific effort over several years and the contributions of many skilled researchers working together.
pieces.about: Herbert H. Anderson was an American organic chemist, a member of Glenn Seaborg's Met Lab group at Chicago during the Manhattan Project. Anderson was a co-inventor, with Larned B. Asprey, of the PUREX process for plutonium and uranium extraction.

As emperor during the Shōwa era, Hirohito oversaw the rise of Japanese militarism, Japan's expansionism in Asia, the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War and World War II, and the postwar Japanese economic miracle.

Igor Kurchatov plays a crucial role in the Soviet side of Sheinkin's story about the race to build and steal atomic weapons:

Soviet Atomic Program Leader: Kurchatov headed the Soviet Union's atomic bomb project, making him the Soviet equivalent of Oppenheimer. His leadership was essential to the USSR's eventual success in developing nuclear weapons.
Intelligence Beneficiary: Kurchatov's program was significantly aided by the atomic secrets stolen by Soviet spies like Klaus Fuchs, Harry Gold, and Ted Hall. The stolen Manhattan Project information helped accelerate Soviet atomic weapons development under Kurchatov's direction.
Cold War Context: Through Kurchatov's efforts, Sheinkin shows how the atomic bomb immediately created a nuclear arms race between the United States and Soviet Union. Kurchatov's success in developing Soviet atomic weapons helped establish the Cold War nuclear standoff.
Scientific Competition: Kurchatov represents the international dimension of atomic weapons development, showing how brilliant scientists in different countries were working simultaneously on similar problems, though the Soviets had the advantage of stolen American research.
Stalin's Pressure: Kurchatov worked under enormous pressure from Stalin to develop atomic weapons quickly, illustrating how political leaders pushed scientists to achieve nuclear capabilities as rapidly as possible.

Igor Kurchatov embodies the Soviet scientific effort to achieve nuclear parity with the United States, representing how the atomic bomb immediately became an international competition and showing how stolen Manhattan Project secrets helped accelerate the global spread of nuclear weapons technology.
pieces.about: Igor Vasilyevich Kurchatov, was a Soviet physicist who played a central role in organizing and directing the former Soviet program of nuclear weapons, and has been referred to as "father of the Russian atomic bomb".

pieces.about: The Institute for Advanced Study (IAS) is an independent center for theoretical research and intellectual inquiry located in Princeton, New Jersey. Robert Oppenheimer, Emmy Noether, Hermann Weyl, John von Neumann, Michael Walzer, Clifford Geertz and Kurt Gödel, many of whom had emigrated from Europe to the United States.

Isidor Rabi plays several important roles in Sheinkin's account of the Manhattan Project:

Scientific Expertise: As one of the leading physicists recruited to Los Alamos, Rabi contributed his expertise in atomic physics to the theoretical and experimental work needed to develop functional atomic weapons.
Moral Voice: Rabi represented the scientists who questioned the ethics of their work, particularly regarding the use of atomic weapons against civilian populations. His concerns reflected the moral struggles many Manhattan Project scientists experienced.
Scientific Community: Through Rabi's interactions with other scientists like Oppenheimer, Fermi, and Bethe, Sheinkin illustrates the collaborative nature of the Manhattan Project and how the world's leading physicists worked together on this unprecedented challenge.
Witness to History: Rabi was present during key moments in the Manhattan Project, including important meetings and decisions about the development and potential use of atomic weapons.
Post-War Reflection: Rabi's later reflections on the Manhattan Project and atomic weapons development help illustrate the lasting impact of the project on the scientists who participated in it.

Isidor Rabi embodies the brilliant scientists who contributed essential expertise to the Manhattan Project while also grappling with the profound moral and ethical questions raised by the creation of atomic weapons, representing the complex feelings of accomplishment and concern that many project participants experienced.
pieces.about: Israel "Isidor" Isaac Rabi was an American nuclear physicist who received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1944 "for his resonance method for recording the magnetic properties of atomic nuclei". He was also one of the first scientists in the United States to work on the cavity magnetron, which is used in microwave radar and microwave ovens.

pieces.about: Jacob Beser was a lieutenant in the United States Army Air Forces who served during World War II. Beser was the radar specialist aboard the Enola Gay on August 6, 1945, when it dropped the Little Boy atomic bomb on Hiroshima. Three days later, Beser was a crewmember aboard Bockscar when the Fat Man bomb was dropped on Nagasaki. He was the only person to have served as a strike crew member of both of the 1945 atomic bomb missions.

pieces.about: James Francis Byrnes was an American judge and politician from South Carolina. A member of the Democratic Party, he served in the U.S. Congress and on the U.S. Supreme Court, as well as in the executive branch, most prominently as the 49th U.S. Secretary of State under President Harry S. Truman. Byrnes was also the 104th governor of South Carolina.

In his capacity with the Health Group, Nolan was placed in charge of safety for the Trinity Test. Safety was not the military’s top priority, however. In Nolan’s own words, “Possible hazards were not too important in those days. There was a war going on.” There was also an incomplete view of all the weapon’s effects: “The bomb was designed as a weapon of warfare primarily utilizing blast and heat for destructive forces…radiation hazards were entirely secondary.”

Nolan’s top priority was recovering data about the blast (radiation-related and otherwise). A secondary role was measuring if there was dangerous radiation, and notifying the proper authorities. 
He had been assigned to another important task: transporting components of the Little Boy bomb to Tinian Island in the Pacific. He and Robert Furman set off on a journey with a crate containing the bomb mechanism and a canister of uranium. Nolan, as a radiation specialist, had been chosen for his ability to monitor the uranium.

Jens Poulsson plays a crucial role in one of the most dramatic and important storylines in Sheinkin's "Bomb" - the Norwegian resistance operations against German heavy water production:

Advance Team Leader: Poulsson led the advance reconnaissance team (codenamed "Grouse") that parachuted into Norway months before the main sabotage operation. His team's job was to gather intelligence on the Vemork plant and prepare for the arrival of British commandos.
Survival Against Odds: When the British commando operation failed disastrously, Poulsson and his team were stranded in the Norwegian wilderness through a brutal winter. Their survival story illustrates the incredible hardships endured by resistance fighters.
Mission Continuity: After the failed British raid, Poulsson helped coordinate with the follow-up Norwegian sabotage team that successfully destroyed the heavy water production facility, demonstrating how persistence and local knowledge could overcome initial failures.
David vs. Goliath Theme: Poulsson's story embodies the book's theme of how small groups of determined individuals could significantly impact the race for atomic weapons. His actions helped prevent Nazi Germany from obtaining crucial materials for atomic research.
International Scope: Through Poulsson's experiences, Sheinkin shows how the atomic bomb race involved people from many nations, not just the major powers' scientists and military leaders.

Poulsson represents the unsung heroes whose courage and sacrifice in remote, dangerous operations were essential to preventing Nazi atomic weapons development.
pieces.about: Jens-Anton Poulsson DSO was a Norwegian military officer. During World War II he was a Norwegian resistance member, especially noted for his role in the heavy water sabotage 1942–1943. He continued his military career after the war, and was appointed colonel in 1968.

pieces.name: Jews
pieces.about: The Jews or Jewish people are an ethnoreligious group and nation originating from the Israelites of the ancient Near East, and whose traditional religion is Judaism. Jewish ethnicity, religion, and community are highly interrelated, as Judaism is an ethnic religion, although not all ethnic Jews practice it. Despite this, religious Jews regard individuals who have formally converted to Judaism as part of the community.

pieces.name: Joachim Rønneberg

Joachim Rønneberg plays a crucial role in one of the most dramatic storylines in Sheinkin's "Bomb" - the Norwegian resistance operations against German heavy water production:

Operation Gunnerside Leader: Rønneberg led the successful Norwegian sabotage mission that destroyed the heavy water electrolysis cells at the Vemork plant in February 1943. This operation was critical in denying Nazi Germany materials needed for atomic research.
Strategic Success: Under Rønneberg's leadership, the team successfully penetrated the heavily guarded facility, placed explosives in precisely the right locations, and escaped without casualties - a remarkable achievement that significantly set back German atomic research.
International Cooperation: Rønneberg's mission represented the successful collaboration between British SOE intelligence, Norwegian resistance fighters, and Allied strategic planning to prevent Nazi atomic weapons development.
David vs. Goliath Theme: His story embodies Sheinkin's broader theme about how small groups of determined individuals could have enormous impact on the atomic weapons race. The success of his mission helped ensure that Germany would not develop atomic weapons first.
Heroic Legacy: Rønneberg and his team's successful destruction of the heavy water production facility became one of the most celebrated sabotage operations of World War II, demonstrating how resistance fighters could strike decisive blows against the Nazi war machine.

Joachim Rønneberg represents the brave resistance leaders whose tactical expertise, courage, and successful execution of dangerous missions were essential to preventing Nazi Germany from obtaining the materials needed for atomic weapons development, ultimately helping to ensure that the Allies would win the race to build the atomic bomb.
pieces.about: Joachim Holmboe Rønneberg was a Norwegian Army officer and broadcaster. He was known for his resistance work during World War II, most notably commanding Operation Gunnerside, and his post-war war information work.

After 11 years in the post, Hoover became instrumental in founding the FBI in June 1935, where he remained as director for an additional 37 years until his death in May 1972 – serving a total of 48 years leading both the BOI and the FBI under eight Presidents.

pieces.about: John Henry Manley was an American physicist who worked with J. Robert Oppenheimer at the University of California, Berkeley before becoming a group leader during the Manhattan Project.

Colonel John Wilson plays a vital role in the Norwegian resistance storyline of Sheinkin's "Bomb":

Intelligence Coordination: His role demonstrates how the race for atomic weapons involved not just scientists in laboratories, but also intelligence officers coordinating complex international operations to prevent enemy atomic weapons development.
Bridge Between Nations: Wilson represented the collaboration between British intelligence and Norwegian resistance fighters, showing how the atomic bomb story involved cooperation across national boundaries in the fight against Nazi Germany.

Colonel Wilson embodies the intelligence and special operations dimension of the atomic weapons race, illustrating how military leaders coordinated dangerous missions that were essential to preventing Nazi atomic weapons development.

pieces.name: Joseph Hirschfelder

Joseph Hirschfelder represents the scientifically responsible voices within the Manhattan Project who worked to understand and warn about the broader consequences of atomic weapons, while also contributing essential technical expertise to their development, embodying the complex moral position of scientists who created weapons of unprecedented destructive power while trying to understand and mitigate their dangers.
pieces.about: Joseph Oakland Hirschfelder was an American physicist who participated in the Manhattan Project and in the creation of the nuclear bomb.

Joseph Stalin serves as the shadowy antagonist driving the Soviet espionage efforts that form one of the central storylines in Sheinkin's "Bomb." While Harry Gold represents the human face of Soviet espionage, Stalin is the ultimate authority who creates the intelligence apparatus that steals American atomic secrets.
In Sheinkin's narrative, Stalin embodies the transformation of nuclear science from international cooperation to national competition. His character shows how the existence of atomic weapons immediately created new forms of international rivalry and espionage, setting the stage for the Cold War nuclear arms race that would define the second half of the 20th century.
Stalin's presence in "Bomb" demonstrates that the atomic age was never just about science or even just about ending World War II - it was immediately about post-war power dynamics and the struggle for nuclear supremacy that would shape global politics for decades to come. His intelligence operations show how atomic secrets became the most valuable currency in international relations, worth the enormous risks taken by spies like Harry Gold and Klaus Fuchs.
pieces.about: Joseph Vissarionovich Stalin was a Soviet politician and revolutionary who led the Soviet Union from 1924 until his death in 1953. He held office as General Secretary of the Communist Party from 1922 to 1952 and as the fourth premier from 1941 until his death. Despite initially governing the country as part of a collective leadership, he ultimately consolidated power to become an absolute dictator by the 1930s. Stalin codified the party's official interpretation of Marxism as Marxism–Leninism, while the totalitarian political system he created is known as Stalinism.

pieces.name: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg
pieces.sentence:
Epilogue: Scorpions in a Bottle: 228

Julius and Ethel Rosenberg play a central role in Steve Sheinkin's "Bomb" as key figures in the Soviet atomic spy network:

Spy Network Leaders - Julius organized and coordinated a spy ring that included David Greenglass (Ethel's brother), who worked at Los Alamos and provided crucial atomic bomb information to the Soviets.
Atomic Intelligence Theft - Through their network, the Rosenbergs helped steal vital information about the atomic bomb's design, including technical drawings and specifications that accelerated Soviet bomb development.
Family Espionage - Their case illustrates how Soviet espionage often operated through family connections, with Ethel's brother David being recruited into spying partly through family relationships.
Cold War Prosecution - The Rosenbergs became symbols of the domestic communist threat during the early Cold War, with their trial and execution representing America's fear of internal subversion.
Ultimate Consequences - Their execution in 1953 demonstrated the deadly serious consequences of atomic espionage and marked a climax in the hunt for atomic spies.
Historical Controversy - Their case became one of the most controversial spy prosecutions in American history, raising questions about justice, evidence, and the death penalty.

Sheinkin uses the Rosenbergs' story to show how atomic espionage tore apart families and communities, and to illustrate the intense fear and paranoia that characterized the early Cold War period when atomic secrets were seen as matters of national survival.
pieces.about: Julius Rosenberg and Ethel Rosenberg were an American married couple who were convicted of spying for the Soviet Union, including providing top-secret information about American radar, sonar, jet propulsion engines, and nuclear weapon designs. They were executed by the federal government of the United States in 1953 using New York's state execution chamber in Sing Sing in Ossining, New York, becoming the first American civilians to be executed for such charges and the first to be executed during peacetime. Other convicted co-conspirators were sentenced to prison, including Ethel's brother, David Greenglass, Harry Gold, and Morton Sobell. Klaus Fuchs, a German scientist working at the Los Alamos Laboratory, was convicted in the United Kingdom. For decades, many people, including the Rosenbergs' sons, have maintained that Ethel was innocent of spying and have sought an exoneration on her behalf from multiple U.S. presidents.

pieces.about: J. Robert Oppenheimer was an American theoretical physicist who served as the director of the Manhattan Project's Los Alamos Laboratory during World War II. He is often called the "father of the atomic bomb" for his role in overseeing the development of the first nuclear weapons.

pieces.about: Karl Eugen Julius Wirtz was a German nuclear physicist, born in Cologne. He was arrested by the allied British and American Armed Forces and incarcerated at Farm Hall for six months in 1945 under Operation Epsilon.

pieces.sentence:
Quiet Fellow: 64
Kitty Oppenheimer plays several important roles in Sheinkin's account of the atomic bomb story:

Los Alamos Life: As the wife of the Manhattan Project's scientific director, Kitty experienced firsthand the isolation, secrecy, and unique community life at Los Alamos. Her presence illustrates the personal sacrifices made by families involved in the project.
Security Concerns: Kitty's past political associations, like Robert's, became part of the suspicions about the Oppenheimer family's loyalty. Her background contributed to the government's concerns about security risks at Los Alamos.
The Chevalier Incident: Kitty was present during the famous dinner with Haakon Chevalier and his wife when the approach about sharing atomic secrets with the Soviets was made. Her presence during this crucial event made her a witness to one of the most damaging episodes in her husband's career.
Personal Cost: Through Kitty's experience, Sheinkin shows how the Manhattan Project affected not just the scientists themselves but their families, who had to live with the secrecy, stress, and eventual moral burden of creating weapons of mass destruction.
Post-War Troubles: Kitty stood by Robert during his later security hearings and the controversy that ultimately stripped him of his security clearance, demonstrating the lasting personal impact of their involvement in the atomic bomb project.

Kitty Oppenheimer represents the family members and spouses who shared in both the achievements and the consequences of the Manhattan Project, showing how the race to build atomic weapons affected entire families and communities, not just the scientists themselves.
pieces.about: Katherine Vissering "Kitty" Oppenheimer was a German-American biologist, botanist, and a member of the Communist Party of America until leaving in the 1930s. Her husbands were Frank Ramseyer, Joe Dallet, Richard Stewart Harrison, and physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, the director of the Manhattan Project's Los Alamos Laboratory during World War II.

pieces.name: Kenneth Bainbridge
pieces.sentence:

Sheinkin uses Bainbridge's story to illustrate the transition from scientific theory to world-changing weapon, and to explore the complex emotions scientists felt when they realized the full implications of their work.
pieces.about: Kenneth Tompkins Bainbridge was an American physicist at Harvard University who worked on cyclotron research. His accurate measurements of mass differences between nuclear isotopes allowed him to confirm Albert Einstein's mass–energy equivalence concept. He was the Director of the Manhattan Project's Trinity nuclear test, which took place July 16, 1945. Bainbridge described the Trinity explosion as a "foul and awesome display". He remarked to J. Robert Oppenheimer immediately after the test, "Now we are all sons of bitches." This marked the beginning of his dedication to ending the testing of nuclear weapons and to efforts to maintain civilian control of future developments in that field.

pieces.name: Kenneth Nichols

Kenneth Nichols embodies the skilled military administrators whose organizational expertise, resource procurement abilities, and engineering knowledge were essential to transforming scientific concepts into functioning weapons production facilities, representing the massive logistical and administrative infrastructure that made the Manhattan Project possible.
pieces.about: Kenneth David Nichols CBE was an officer in the United States Army, and a civil engineer who worked on the secret Manhattan Project, which developed the atomic bomb during World War II. He served as Deputy District Engineer to James C. Marshall, and from 13 August 1943 as the District Engineer of the Manhattan Engineer District. Nichols led both the uranium production facility at the Clinton Engineer Works at Oak Ridge, Tennessee, and the plutonium production facility at Hanford Engineer Works in Washington state.

pieces.about: The Committee for State Security was the main security agency for the Soviet Union from 13 March 1954 until 3 December 1991. As a direct successor of preceding agencies such as the Cheka, GPU, OGPU, NKGB, NKVD and MGB, it was attached to the Council of Ministers. It was the chief government agency of "union-republican jurisdiction", carrying out internal security, foreign intelligence, counter-intelligence and secret police functions. Similar agencies operated in each of the republics of the Soviet Union aside from the Russian SFSR, where the KGB was headquartered, with many associated ministries, state committees and state commissions.

pieces.about: Klaus Emil Julius Fuchs was a theoretical physicist, atomic spy, and communist who supplied information from the American, British, and Canadian Manhattan Project to the Soviet Union during and shortly after World War II. While at the Los Alamos Laboratory, Fuchs was responsible for many significant theoretical calculations relating to the first nuclear weapons and, later, early models of the hydrogen bomb. After his conviction in 1950, he served nine years in prison in the United Kingdom, then migrated to East Germany where he resumed his career as a physicist and scientific leader.

pieces.name: Knut Haugland
pieces.sentence:
Gliders Down: 55
Knut Haugland plays an important role in the Norwegian resistance operations that form a crucial subplot in Sheinkin's "Bomb":

Communications Lifeline: As the radio operator for the Norwegian resistance teams, Haugland was responsible for maintaining contact between the field operatives and British SOE headquarters in London. His communications work was vital for coordinating the timing and execution of sabotage operations.
Grouse/Swallow Team Member: Haugland was part of the advance reconnaissance team that parachuted into Norway to prepare for the sabotage missions against the Vemork heavy water plant. His role was essential to the success of subsequent operations.
Long-term Survival: When operations were delayed or failed, Haugland had to survive in the Norwegian wilderness for extended periods, maintaining radio contact and keeping the mission alive despite enormous hardships.
Heavy Water Sabotage: His communications work supported both the failed British commando raid and the successful Norwegian Operation Gunnerside that ultimately destroyed the German heavy water production facility.
David vs. Goliath Theme: Haugland's story exemplifies how small groups of dedicated individuals could significantly impact the race for atomic weapons through their specialized skills and unwavering commitment.

Haugland represents the crucial but often overlooked technical specialists whose expertise in communications and other support roles made complex resistance operations possible, demonstrating how the atomic weapons race required diverse skills beyond just scientific knowledge.
pieces.about: Knut Magne Haugland, DSO, MM, was a resistance fighter and noted explorer from Norway, who accompanied Thor Heyerdahl on his famous 1947 Kon-Tiki expedition.

Knut Haukelid represents the third major storyline that Sheinkin focuses on - the Norwegian resistance efforts to sabotage German bomb development. His story is crucial to the book's narrative because it shows how the race to build the atomic bomb wasn't just about American and Soviet scientific efforts, but also about preventing the Germans from succeeding first. His story serves as a counterpoint to the American scientific race and Soviet espionage efforts, showing how the battle for atomic supremacy involved direct military action to prevent enemy scientific progress, not just scientific advancement and intelligence gathering.
Haukelid's role spans multiple critical operations: he was supposed to be part of Operation Grouse in 1942 but was injured, then during Operation Gunnerside he served as second in command and headed the cover group during the successful sabotage of the Vemork heavy water plant. His actions directly contributed to blocking the Germans from producing and shipping "heavy water," essential to their objective of developing the atomic bomb, and "gave the United States time to complete their own atomic bomb.
pieces.about: Knut Haukelid was an American-born Norwegian military officer. He was a Norwegian resistance movement soldier during World War II, most notable for participating in the Norwegian heavy water sabotage.

pieces.name: Knut Lier-Hansen
pieces.sentence:
Ferry Job: 110

Knut Lier-Hansen plays an important role in one of the most dramatic storylines in Sheinkin's "Bomb" - the Norwegian resistance operations against German heavy water production:

Operation Gunnerside Participant: Lier-Hansen was one of the Norwegian saboteurs who successfully destroyed the heavy water electrolysis cells at the Vemork plant in February 1943. This operation was crucial in denying Nazi Germany the materials needed for atomic research.
Technical Expertise: His knowledge of explosives and sabotage techniques was essential for the precise destruction of the heavy water equipment, requiring careful placement of charges to damage the production facility without causing unnecessary casualties.
Dangerous Escape: After the successful sabotage mission, Lier-Hansen had to survive the perilous escape across occupied Norwegian territory, evading German patrols and surviving in harsh winter conditions.
David vs. Goliath Theme: Lier-Hansen's story embodies Sheinkin's broader theme about how small groups of determined individuals could have enormous impact on the atomic weapons race. His actions helped prevent Nazi atomic weapons development.
International Cooperation: His mission represented the successful collaboration between British SOE intelligence, Norwegian resistance fighters, and Allied strategic planning to prevent Nazi Germany from obtaining crucial atomic research materials.

Knut Lier-Hansen represents the brave Norwegian resistance fighters whose specialized skills, courage, and successful execution of dangerous sabotage missions were essential to preventing Nazi Germany from obtaining the heavy water needed for atomic weapons research, helping to ensure that the Allies would win the race to develop nuclear weapons.
pieces.about:
Knut Lier-Hansen was a Norwegian resistance member during World War II.
He was born and grew up in Rjukan. Around 1940 he was a sergeant in the Norwegian Army, and tried to repel the German invaders in April 1940, among others in a skirmish at Gransherad. He later joined the more irregular resistance movement. His most notable mission was the sinking of SF Hydro as a part of the Norwegian heavy water sabotage. After placing explosives below deck in the ferry, the saboteurs had to wait until the ferry's departure in the morning to oversee that nothing went against the plan. After witnessing the ferry leave harbor in a normal way, Lier-Hansen fled the scene for Einar Skinnarland's house. The ferry went down in the middle of Lake Tinn, and in addition to sabotaging the heavy water program, eighteen lives were lost. When the war between Germany and Norway was over, on 8 May 1945, Lier-Hansen was dispatched together with Henry Johansen and another person to arrest Reichskommissar für die besetzten Norwegischen Gebiete Josef Terboven. The Norwegians reached Skaugum where Terboven had entrenched himself, but they were warded off by guards. Soon after, Terboven blew himself up.

pieces.about: Lavrentiy Pavlovich Beria was a Soviet politician and one of the longest-serving and most influential of Joseph Stalin's secret police chiefs, serving as head of the NKVD from 1938 to 1946, during the country's involvement in the Second World War.

Lee DuBridge represents the broader scientific community that supported and witnessed the Manhattan Project, providing crucial observations about key figures like Oppenheimer while also illustrating how the atomic bomb effort drew on the expertise and collaboration of scientists from major research institutions across the United States.
pieces.about: Lee Alvin DuBridge was an American educator and physicist, best known as president of the California Institute of Technology from 1946 to 1969.

pieces.name: Leona Woods

Leona Woods embodies the brilliant young scientists whose technical expertise and personal dedication were essential to the Manhattan Project's success, while also representing the unique challenges faced by women in wartime scientific research and their crucial but often overlooked contributions to creating the atomic bomb.
pieces.about: Leona Harriet Woods, later known as Leona Woods Marshall and Leona Woods Marshall Libby, was an American physicist who helped build the first nuclear reactor and the first atomic bomb.

pieces.name: Leonid Kvasnikov
pieces.sentence:

Sheinkin uses Kvasnikov's story to show the sophisticated and organized nature of Soviet atomic espionage, demonstrating how the USSR deployed professional intelligence officers to systematically steal the secrets that would help them develop their own atomic weapons and achieve nuclear parity with the United States.
pieces.about: Leonid Romanovich Kvasnikov was a Soviet and Russian chemical engineer and a spy, serving first in NKVD and later served in KGB. Graduated with honors from the Moscow Institute of Chemical Machine-Building in 1934 and worked as an engineer in a chemical plant for several years in the Tula region. Kvasnikov continued postgraduate engineering studies and joined the KGB in 1938 as a specialist in scientific-technical intelligence. Beginning in 1939 he was the section head of scientific and technical intelligence. Kvasnikov served a few short-term assignments in Germany and Poland and rising swiftly to become deputy chief and then chief of the KGB scientific intelligence section.

pieces.name: Leo Szilard

Leo Szilard, a Jewish Hungarian physicist, appears as a pivotal figure who sets the entire story in motion. He represents the scientific conscience that both launches and questions the atomic project He serves as a crucial bridge character in Sheinkin's narrative, connecting the theoretical scientific breakthrough to the political decision-making that launched the Manhattan Project. Szilard "wrote the letter for Albert Einstein's signature" and "with the assistance of colleagues Albert Einstein, Edward Teller, and Eugene Wigner, wrote the famous 'Einstein Letter' warning President Franklin Roosevelt" about the German nuclear threat.
pieces.about: Leo Szilard was a Hungarian-born physicist, biologist and inventor who made numerous important discoveries in nuclear physics and the biological sciences. He conceived the nuclear chain reaction in 1933, and patented the idea in 1936. In late 1939 he wrote the letter for Albert Einstein's signature that resulted in the Manhattan Project that built the atomic bomb, and then in 1945 wrote the Szilard petition asking president Harry S. Truman to demonstrate the bomb without dropping it on civilians. According to György Marx, he was one of the Hungarian scientists known as The Martians.

pieces.name: Leslie Groves
pieces.sentence:
Chain Reactions: 42
